en: Samantabhadra: The *Āptamīmāṃsā* [states]:
"The divine arrivals, celestial vehicles, yak-tail whisks, and other such splendors—"
They are seen even among those who employ illusion; therefore, you are not great to us.
This great manifestation of the body and so forth exists internally and externally;
it is divine and real even among the denizens of heaven, yet it persists even in those possessed of passion and other defilements.

And because the systems of the various founders of religious traditions contradict one another, none of them possesses the status of an authoritative teacher; rather, there must be someone who alone is the true Guru.
The complete elimination of defects and obscurations occurs because of the possibility of excellence,
just as in certain cases there is the total destruction of external and internal impurities due to their own specific causes.
Just as objects that are subtle, concealed, or distant are perceptible to someone because they are inferable— such as fire and the like— so too is the existence of an omniscient being established.
You alone are faultless, for your speech does not contradict reason or scripture;
there is no contradiction when that which you assert is not sublated by what is commonly established.
For those who stand outside the nectar of your doctrine, who are proponents of absolute monism in every respect,
and who are consumed by the conceit of being authoritative persons, their own cherished views are sublated by what is perceived through direct experience.
O Protector, for those who are attached to extremist views and act as enemies to themselves and others, there is no such thing as wholesome or unwholesome karma, nor is there a future world anywhere.
If existence were absolute, there would be a denial of non-existent things;
therefore, your [view] is devoid of its own nature—being the soul of all, without beginning or end.
If the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) were denied, the effect-substance would be beginningless;
and if the property of destruction (pradhvaṃsa) were lost, it would become infinite.
If there were no exclusion of others (anyāpoha), that single entity would have to consist of all things;
otherwise, it would be designated in every way through inherence (samavāya).

Even in the view of those who maintain the absolute non-existence of all things and deny the reality of existence, by what means could their statements of cognition, their proofs, or their refutations be established as valid? (Sām̐khyakārikā 12)
For those who hate the logic of *syādvāda*, there can be no identity of both [existence and non-existence] due to contradiction;
even in the absolute position of ineffability, the statement "it is ineffable" is not tenable.

In some way that [object] is desired by you as existent, in some way it is non-existent, and likewise it is both or inexpressible; this is due to the application of [different] perspectives, not in every respect.
Who would not desire that everything is real, given its fourfold nature consisting of its own form and so forth? If it were unreal due to error, it could not be established as such.
From the two [aspects] presented in succession, duality arises; "both" and "inexpressible" arise from an inability [to express them simultaneously].
From their own respective causes, the remaining three propositions follow after the "inexpressible."
Existence is invariably concomitant with that which is to be negated within a single substratum;
because it serves as a qualifier, it constitutes a similarity [of properties], just as in the case of the desire to express distinction.
Non-existence is invariably concomitant with that which is to be negated within a single substratum;
because it functions as a qualifier, it constitutes a dissimilarity, just as in the case where non-difference is intended to be expressed.
The qualified object (viśeṣya), which consists of both the thing to be enjoined and the thing to be prohibited, is the domain of words;
it is like the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), which is both a reason (hetu) and a non-reason (ahetu) depending on the perspective.
The remaining alternative positions (bhaṅgas) should also be understood through the application of the logic already stated;
O Lord of Munis, there is no contradiction whatsoever in your teaching.

If it is argued that, because of such injunctions and prohibitions, the object is not established as having causal efficacy, we say no; for its efficacy exists according to its effects through external and internal limiting conditions (upādhis).
In each and every property (dharma), the meaning is distinct from that of the substratum (dharmī) which possesses infinite properties;
when one particular aspect is primary, the remaining aspects function as its subordinate members.
One who is expert in the methods [of reasoning] should apply this same analytical procedure—characterized by the refutation of unity and plurality—to all subsequent [arguments] as well. 23.
Even in the doctrine of the absolute non-duality (advaita), observed diversity is contradicted;
for neither the causal factors nor the action arises from itself as a single entity.
There would be no duality of karma, no duality of fruits, and no duality of worlds;
likewise, there would be no duality of knowledge and ignorance, nor any duality of bondage and liberation.
If the establishment of non-duality were achieved through a logical reason, then duality would exist between the reason and the probandum;
if, on the other hand, it were established without a reason, why is it not merely a matter of words?
Non-duality does not exist without duality, just as a non-cause cannot exist without a cause;
for one who possesses a name, there is no negation anywhere without that which is to be negated.

Even in the view that difference is absolute, if there were no non-difference from difference, then difference itself would not exist as difference; for this quality [of difference] resides in many things.
The continuum, the collection, unrestricted similarity, and rebirth—all these would not exist if the identity [of the person] were denied. (SAṃ 29)
If knowledge were distinct from the knower by its very nature, then knowledge would be non-existent in two ways [as separate from the object].
In the absence of knowledge, how could there be an object of knowledge for you opponents, whether external or internal?
The words of others have general meaning, and no particularity is expressed;
because they lack a universal [referent], all their words are indeed false.
For those who hate the logic of *syādvāda*, there can be no single nature consisting of both [existence and non-existence] due to contradiction;
even in the absolute position of ineffability, the statement "it is inexpressible" is not tenable.
In that which is independent, distinctness and unity are indeed non-entities because they arise from two causes;
for example, the proof of that very unity and distinctness through its own internal divisions.

But because of the commonality of "being," there is the oneness of all things; yet due to the distinctions of separate substances and so forth, one may intend to express either difference or non-difference, just as in the case of a unique cause.

For those seekers of that [truth], there is both the desire to express and the lack of desire to express a real qualifier here with respect to the qualified object, which possesses infinite attributes; however, there is no such desire for a non-existent qualifier.
Difference and non-difference, being within the scope of valid cognition, are not merely conventional;
these two are not contradictory in one and the same thing when intended respectively as the subordinate and the primary.
Even under the view of absolute permanence, transformation is not possible;
how much less so the absence of causal agents—where, then, could there be a means of knowledge, and where its fruit?
If that which is manifested by the means of valid cognition and the causal factors is indeed manifest, just like the sense organs and their objects,
then why would that which is eternally subject to modification be outside the teaching of the Sublime One?
If the existent is in every way incapable of arising like a person,
then the postulation of transformation (pariṇāma) contradicts the absolute nature of permanence.
For those for whom you are not their leader, there would be no performance of meritorious or sinful deeds, how could there be rebirth or its fruit, and neither bondage nor liberation?
Even in the view that things are exclusively momentary, rebirth and so forth are impossible;
since there is no recognition and the like, how could there be the commencement of an action, and whence its fruit? (Sām̐khyakārikā 41)

If the effect were non-existent in every respect, then let it not arise, like a sky-flower; let there be no restriction regarding its material cause, and let there be no confidence in the production of an effect.
The relationship between cause and effect and so forth does not exist [as a single entity], because it lacks continuity due to being distinct from other entities;
like another continuum, a continuum is not one with that which possesses it, as it is separate from it.
How can this term "non-other" applied to other things not be conventional and false?
There is no conventionality without a primary referent, and there is no conventionality apart from the primary.
Because it is impossible to express any of the four alternatives regarding conceptualization,
the identity or difference between those two— the continuum and its possessor— is inexpressible.
Let even the conceptualization of the fourfold alternative of the inexpressible not be spoken of;
for that which is not all-encompassing would be a non-entity, lacking both the qualified and the qualifier.
The negation of an existing named object occurs through its distinction from substances and so forth;
however, this is not a non-existent difference, for existence is the locus of both affirmation and negation.
A thing would be non-existent and inexpressible, devoid of all extremes;
indeed, a thing becomes a non-thing through the reversal of its conventional process.
If all extremes are inexpressible, then what is the purpose of speaking of them?
If they are conventional reality, this is merely false, because it is the opposite of ultimate reality.

Is it inexpressible because of impossibility, or because of non-existence, or because of lack of cognition? These two initial statements would not be possible; why speak with such pretexts? Speak clearly.
One who acts without intent does not harm; one who possesses intent harms.
The mind that is free from these two is bound; a bound mind is not liberated.
Since destruction is causeless, the cause of violence is not the perpetrator;
furthermore, liberation is the cessation of the mental continuum, and it does not have the eightfold path as its cause.
If the collection of causes for the commencement of a dissimilar effect were not distinct from its substrata, it would be illogical, as there would be no distinction [from the previous state].
The aggregates and the continuums, being conventional, are unconditioned;
for them, there would be no abiding, arising, or passing away, just like the horn of a donkey.
For those who hate the logic of *syādvāda*, neither a single identity consisting of both [existence and non-existence] is possible due to contradiction;
nor is it logical to say "it is inexpressible" within the absolute position of inexpressibility itself.
It is eternal because of the recognition of it; it is not so by chance or due to its non-interruption.
It is momentary because of the difference in time, owing to the fault that [otherwise] there would be no transition of cognition.
It does not arise nor does it perish in its nature as a universal, because its persistence is manifest; yet it perishes and arises through its particularities.
Thus, arising and so forth exist simultaneously in one and the same thing.

The production of an effect and its destruction are distinct from the cause by virtue of their specific characteristics and their fixed nature; yet, because they persist as categories such as "birth" and so forth, they are not independent [of a substratum], for they would otherwise be like a flower in the sky.
Seeking a jar, a crown, or gold, people undergo grief, delusion, and indifference respectively toward their destruction, production, and persistence, each for its own cause.
One who is under the vow of milk does not eat curd; one under the vow of curd does not drink milk; one under the vow of non-dairy products eats neither. Therefore, reality consists of these three.

If the diversity between cause and effect, as well as the distinction between quality and the possessor of quality, and the difference between a universal and its instances, are asserted to be absolute; 61.
A single [entity] cannot reside in many [locations], because it lacks parts; nor can it have many [parts], because it would then possess parts.
Consequently, its unity is lost; thus, for one who does not accept [the existence of] atoms, there is a fault regarding the mode of subsistence.
Even with respect to differences in place and time, there would be coexistence as in the case of "joined-accomplishment" (yutasiddhi);
however, there could be no common location for a material cause and its effect.
"Because of the relationship between substratum and superstratum, there is no independence for those things that possess inherence;
thus, that relation is untenable, as it is not logically consistent with the possessors of inherence. (SāmK 64)
Since both the universal and inherence are entirely contained within each individual instance, they could not exist without a substratum; what rule, then, would govern their destruction and arising?
In every respect, there is no connection between the universal and inherence; nor is the object connected with those two. Thus, these three are like flowers in the sky.
If atoms were absolutely non-different [from one another], then even in a composite, they would remain uncombined, just as they are when separated;
thus, the fourfold primary elements would be nothing but an illusion.
The error regarding the effect is the error regarding the atom, for the cause is indeed known through its effect;
because both [the atom and its qualities] are absent, that which resides therein is neither a quality nor a genus.
If there were oneness, there would be the absence of one of the two, the absence of the remainder, and the absence of that which is invariably concomitant;
furthermore, it would contradict the number two. If you say this is merely conventional, then it is simply false.
For those who hate the logic of *syādvāda*, neither a single nature consisting of both [existence and non-existence] is possible due to contradiction;
nor is it tenable to say "it is inexpressible" within the absolute position of inexpressibility itself.
There is identity between substance and its modes because they are not distinct from one another,
and because of their specific transformation, as well as the relationship between the possessor of power and the power itself.
Due to differences in designation and number, due to differences in specific characteristics,
and due to differences in purpose and so forth, its multiplicity is not absolute.
If establishment were dependent, the two would not be established;
and if establishment were non-dependent, there could be no relationship between the universal and the particular.
For those who hate the logic of the *syādvāda*, there can be no single identity of both [existence and non-existence] due to contradiction;
even in the absolute position of ineffability, the statement "it is inexpressible" is not tenable.
The inseparable connection between the property and the locus is established through mutual observation;
for this [connection] does not exist by its own nature, just like the factors of an agent or a means of cognition.
If everything were established through a logical reason, there would be no comprehension [of it] through perception and so forth;
if everything were established through scripture, then even doctrines with contradictory meanings would be established.
For those who hate the logic of the *syādvāda*, neither the identity of both [existence and non-existence] is possible due to contradiction;
even in the absolute position of ineffability, the statement "it is inexpressible" is not tenable.
When the speaker is untrustworthy, that which is to be proven by means of a reason is established by that reason;
when the speaker is trustworthy, that which is to be proven from his statement is established by scripture.
If the ultimate internal reality is held to be exclusively [ineffable], then every word of the Buddha is false; therefore, it is merely a semblance of a means of valid cognition.
Without such a means of valid cognition, how [could that reality be known]?
If the state of representation-only consists in the cognition of the object to be proven and the means of proof,
then there is neither a thesis nor a reason, due to the fallacies of the proposition and the reason.

If there were an absolute adherence to the external object as the sole reality, then all those who propound contradictory meanings would achieve their purpose, because they could simply deny that their statements are fallacious cognitions.
For those who hate the logic of *syādvāda*, there can be no single identity of both [existence and non-existence] due to contradiction;
even in the absolute position of ineffability, the statement "it is ineffable" is not tenable.

When there is regard for internal objects of cognition (*bhāvaprameya*), there is the negation of fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*); when there is regard for external objects of cognition, you [Dignāga] have both valid means of knowledge and their semblances (*tannibha*).

The word "living being" (jīva) possesses an external referent because it is a conventional designation, just like words that denote causes; likewise, designations for illusions and other errors possess their respective external referents, such as illusions and so forth, just like words that express things as they are.
Those three—intellect, word, and object—are the designations that denote intellect and the rest;
and the three cognitions of intellect and the rest are likewise similar, being reflections of those [objects].
For the speaker, the listener, and the cognizer, the sentences, the cognitions, and the valid cognitions are distinct;
they are indeed errors when there is error regarding valid cognition, whether the external objects are of such a nature or otherwise.
The validity of cognition and verbal testimony depends upon the existence of an external object, not its non-existence;
thus, the distinction between the true and the false is established based on the attainment or non-attainment of the object.
If the accomplishment of one's goal comes from fate alone, how can it be due to human effort?
If it comes from fate, there would be no liberation, and human effort would be fruitless.
If success comes from human effort alone, how can that effort arise from destiny?
If it comes from human effort, then human effort would be unfailing for all living beings.
For those who hate the logic of the *syādvāda*, neither a single identity consisting of both [existence and non-existence] is possible due to contradiction;
nor is it tenable to say "it is inexpressible" within the absolute position of inexpressibility itself.
When there is no prior reliance on conscious deliberation, what is desirable or undesirable comes from one's own destiny;
when there is reliance on prior conscious deliberation, what is desirable or undesirable comes from one's own human effort.
If evil were necessarily [the result] of suffering for others and merit of happiness,
then even insentient things and those free from passions would be bound by virtue of that cause.
If merit were inherently certain to arise from suffering, and evil from happiness,
then the wise sage who has transcended passion would be bound by those two through their very causes.
For those who hate the logic of *syādvāda*, there can be no single nature consisting of both [existence and non-existence] due to contradiction;
nor is it tenable to say "it is inexpressible" within the absolute position of inexpressibility itself.

If the factors of purification and affliction, as well as pleasure and pain residing in oneself and others, are held to be the causes of merit, demerit, and the outflows, then [your doctrine] is logical; otherwise, it is useless for an Arhat.
If bondage were certain due to ignorance, then because the objects of knowledge are infinite, there would be no liberated one (kevalin).
If liberation occurred from a small amount of knowledge, then it would be otherwise—that is, bondage would result—from a great amount of ignorance.
For those who hate the logic of *syādvāda*, neither a single nature consisting of both [existence and non-existence] is possible due to contradiction;
nor is it tenable to say "it is inexpressible" within the absolute position of inexpressibility itself.
Bondage arises from ignorance and delusion, not from ignorance alone for one who is free from delusion;
liberation comes even from a small amount of knowledge when one is free from delusion, whereas otherwise, one remains deluded.
The diverse [world] arises from desire and so forth, in accordance with the bondage of karma;
that karma arises from its own causes, and those living beings [arise] from purity and impurity.
Furthermore, purity and impurity are two powers, like the capacities for being cooked and not being cooked;
their manifestations are beginningless and eternal, and their intrinsic nature is beyond the scope of logical reasoning.
For you, the knowledge of reality is valid cognition that manifests all things simultaneously;
and that knowledge which arises sequentially is refined by the method of the doctrine of manifoldness (syādvāda).

Equanimity is the fruit of the first [power]; for the remaining [powers], it is the cognition of what is to be acquired and what is to be abandoned, or else the prior destruction of ignorance regarding their respective objects.
The particle *syāt* indicates non-absolutism in sentences; because it is connected with meaning, it serves as a qualifier for that which is to be understood, even in the case of your Kevalins.

Syādvāda, arising from the connection with the various modes of absolute one-sidedness, is a formulation of inquiry using the interrogative particle *kim*; it relies upon the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅga*) and the methods of reasoning (*naya*), and distinguishes between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted.
Between the Syādvāda and the Kevalajñāna, which reveal all principles, there is a distinction consisting of being direct and indirect; for otherwise, one of them would necessarily be a non-entity.

A *naya* is that which, through similarity with what possesses similar properties, reveals the specific distinctions of an object analyzed according to the *syādvāda*, because it is not in contradiction [with the whole]. (Sām 106)
The synthesis of all possible modes of presentation— positive and negative— pertaining to the three times,
which constitutes the undivided connection of existents, is the single substance in its manifold aspects.
If you argue that a collection of false [standpoints] is itself false, then for us there is no such thing as absolute falsity.
Standpoints (*naya*) are false when independent; when they are mutually dependent, they constitute the real object that accomplishes its purpose.
An object is restricted by a sentence through either an injunction or a prohibition;
otherwise, it would necessarily lack the quality of being qualified.
Whether it be that very thing or something else, this speech instructs that "it is that very thing.
If it were not true because of its false words, how could there be a teaching on the meaning of reality?
The nature of speech is unrestrained in negating the meaning of other words;
yet it expresses its own object as a universal, and such an object of expression is like a sky-flower.
If it is argued that general speech is not the meaning of words because it refers to particulars, then that [general speech] is indeed not false;
for since it leads to the attainment of the intended particular, the word "syāt" (perhaps/may be) is the hallmark of truth.

That which is to be practiced, which is a constituent part of the desired goal, and which is opposed to negation—likewise, that which is to be accepted or rejected; such is the established position of the *syādvāda*.
Thus, this authoritative Mīmāṃsā has been set forth by one desiring the welfare [of others],
for the purpose of correctly understanding the distinction between right and false teachings.
Victorious in this world is the dustless Lord of Ascetics, the moon that dispels the expansion of the afflictions of worldly existence,

the sun of the methods of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and perspective (*naya*) that has dispelled the darkness of false and one-sided doctrines— [he] from whom [others] cannot even touch the mere droplets of the ocean of his philosophical systems.
The non-Buddhists, clinging to their own views, worship various other [deities].
